682.t: Artists adjusting to orchestras and vocal booth comforts

You can’t suddenly change unless like you do a vocal with a rhythm section and you know they’re going to add strings or horns or something like that. Then…

682.t: Most enjoyable artists: Peggy Lee and prepared artists
682.s: Hank says the best sessions come when artists arrive prepared, citing Peggy Lee, and contrasts those who work everything out in the studio.
682.q: The enjoyable experience is when the artists really come in knowing what they want to do. Like I worked with Peggy Lee — always on time, always ready. Always she had the tune down. You know everything, no problems, we just did it. And there’s those artists

961.t: What Sarah Vaughan was like to accompany
961.s: She was the easiest singer to work with: professional, never complaining, giving great harmonic freedom, an excellent pianist, but repeating her sets.
961.ch: Singers: Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald
961.q: The easiest singer I’ve ever worked with, of any I can think of. I mean just absolutely professional. I never heard Sarah complain once about anything, unless it was a legitimate mess-up, if a sound man or a lighting man or someone wasn’t taking care of business and doing their job, she’d be all…

961.t: Getting the job with Sarah Vaughan

961.ch: Singers: Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald
961.q: I’m never really sure. I was with her two years, two separate years. I worked with her 12 months in ‘79 and then left and went back in ‘83 and worked another full year. But I think I probably initially got the job through Roy McCurdy who was a good friend of mine and we had played together a lot…

961.t: Ella Fitzgerald compared with Sarah, and Ella's stage nerves
961.s: Ella needed more specific accompaniment than the bebop-minded Sarah, and was nervous backstage but fine once on stage.
961.ch: Singers: Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald
961.q: So you have to, to keep it interesting for everybody, you have to try to find interesting little switches on things and a new take on something. So that’s a challenge. When you’re doing new material all the time you don’t maybe even have the time to think about that kind of stuff. So it was great.…

703.t: Buddy Collette, Red Callender and singers of that era
703.s: Portraits of Collette and Callender, his sister's crush, and the high vocal standards set by Sarah Vaughan.
703.ch: Influences, Los Angeles scene and technique
703.q: Buddy Collette, because Buddy Collette used to play a lot with Harold Land. Unbelievable gentleman. I always thought jazz was – at that time, you had to have this little attitude, a little edge on all the time. Buddy Collette was the epitome of a gentleman. “Oh yes, yes son.” Always a big smile,…

703.t: Nina Simone's directions on the bandstand

703.q: She’s [Henderson makes a swatting sound]. “What are we going to play?” “Read the magazine.” “What magazine?” “What are we going to play?” “I don’t know. Read the magazine.” “What key?” “Read the magazine.” [Hutcherson makes another swatting sound.] “Okay.” “Just be ready.” “Can I sing?” “Okay.…

703.t: Carmen McRae as the ultimate singer
703.s: He praises her piano playing and her ability to sing at conversation volume.
703.q: Carmen was the ultimate singer. I loved Carmen because she was a wonderful pianist. Carmen could play the hell out of the piano. She’d say, “Hey, excuse me, here, check this out,” not only say what it has to be, but demonstrate it. There it is. Carmen McRae. You know what I liked about Carmen…

227.s: Mandel prefers intimate singers such as Peggy Lee, Shirley Horn, Billie Holiday and Carmen McRae to belters, and says Sinatra has no peer.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Oh yeah, Peggy Lee for openers. Shirley Horn, I like singers that sound like they are singing in your ear. I don't like belters particularly that's a personal… but I can admire belters, I just don't like being yelled at, especially in love songs.

227.t: Stan Getz's Voices album and vocal groups

227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs

227.t: Understated singers: Helen Merrill, Sade and others

227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs

321.s: He worked with Chet Baker after Woody Herman and Maureen McGovern earlier; Chet sang to set the mood, which taught him restraint.

840.s: Back in Las Vegas he played the Dunes lounge and an after-hours jazz gig. Gus Mancuso recommended him to Sarah Vaughan, and he describes the pianists and the trio with Jimmy Cobb and Carl Schroeder.

358.s: Asked about backing Joe Williams, Simmons explains accompaniment as instant arrangement, learned from Ellington's band and Carmen McRae.

And listening to Duke Ellington, the one thing I noticed is I said that I tried to imitate his band on the piano. And I noticed just right away the individuality of the people in his group as soloists, and how…

851.t: Accompanying singers: Dianne Reeves and Dave Bartholomew
851.s: He discusses intimate accompaniment, great accompanists, rescuing Bartholomew's dropped beat on radio, and Dr. John's musicianship.

613.t: Bing Crosby and when a singer is a musician
613.s: Yanow would amend his old line about Crosby, saying singers are generally musicians and some are show biz performers.
613.q: Well I guess I would amend that statement too, because that was written like twenty years ago. I think I would say he was the first white jazz singer, important white jazz singer who was not an instrumentalist. Because singers are generally musicians too, it’s just that some of them are good…

494.t: The Traveler vocal project and Janice Jarrett's lyrics
